subject: Career
title: The One-Page Rule Myth
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The One-Page Rule Myth.

hook.text: Career advisors insist: one page only. But a study of 6,000 resumes tells a different story.

buildup.text: ResumeGo found two-page resumes got 2.3x more interviews than one-pagers for senior roles.

discovery.text: The real rule isn't page count — it's relevance density. Every line must earn its space.

twist.text: A bloated two-pager is worse than a tight one-pager. Length without substance kills.

climax.text: Entry-level: one page. Mid-career and above: two is fine if every bullet hits.

punchline.text: It's not about pages. It's about wasted lines.

quiz.question: What did a ResumeGo study find about two-page resumes?

details.summary: The one-page resume rule is a guideline, not an absolute law. For early career professionals, one page is appropriate, but experienced professionals with ten or more years of relevant experience may need two pages to adequately convey their qualifications.
details.whyItMatters: Forcing extensive experience onto one page through tiny fonts or removed content can make your resume less readable and less competitive than a clean two-page version.
takeaways: One page is ideal for fewer than ten years of experience
Two pages are acceptable for senior professionals with extensive backgrounds
Every line must earn its space regardless of the page count

faq.question: When is a two-page resume actually better than a one-page resume?
faq.answer: When you have more than ten years of relevant experience, multiple significant accomplishments that demonstrate your qualifications, or when the role requires diverse skills that cannot be adequately shown in one page. The second page must contain high-value content, not filler.

faq.question: What should you cut first if your resume exceeds the appropriate length?
faq.answer: Remove outdated skills that are no longer relevant, positions held more than fifteen years ago unless they are critical, generic job duties that do not show impact, and any information that is not relevant to the target role..
